title: One-Minute Chan Samādhi
excerpt: (A simple, direct method of samādhi by Mr. Wang Xianglu)

inline.s: (A simple, direct method of samādhi by Mr. Wang Xianglu)
After one minute, the bell will sound. You may right-click the triangular Play button to set the audio to loop from the menu, or download the audio file and play it yourself.

In the scorching heat of a long summer, in moods of stifling vexation; when worldly affairs are turned topsy-turvy and nothing can be set right — use the single word “Cut!” (slap!) At once let body and mind both drop away! Instantly become like wood and stone,
with not a single thought arising
(and do not cling even to this writing),
and yet seeing and hearing remain perfectly clear
Look — what is this?

At this moment think neither of good nor of evil, being neither empty nor existent. After one minute of this, rouse your mind again and return to your work. What harm to your affairs? What harm to your time? This one moment alone brings benefits beyond all telling. Why not gladly do it once!

[The “Cut” method] You may also do it this way: speak the single word “Cut!”, then hold the state of no-thought for one minute. [Look — what is this?] This is precisely the Chan method the Sixth Patriarch transmitted to Huiming: “Think neither of good nor of evil — at just this moment, what is your original face, Venerable Ming?” (Translation: Think neither of good nor of evil; at this very moment, when not a single thought arises, which one is your original face? For details see
A Detailed Commentary on the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

Likewise, in moments of joy and delight, when body and mind feel light and you could dance for gladness, you may just as well cut once. The benefit gained is beyond all telling. Why not gladly do it once!

Try it many times a day, and before long you will naturally attain the state of quiescent ease and light tranquillity. Then your original face will be realized of itself, and the three powers of samādhi, wisdom, and emptiness will awaken on their own. The only worry is that you will not be willing to do it. If you can snatch a little leisure amid your busyness, each time you practice it once you grow more adept, until you can dwell in samādhi at every moment and recite the Buddha’s name at every hour, merging them into one seamless whole.
On that final day, your right mindfulness will be clear and bright
. The terror in your heart and the pain in your body will dissolve at once, because your old debts and past karma will already have been cleared away one after another,
and you will even be able to know beforehand the hour of your departure
. Among our fellow practitioners, many have already borne true witness to this
(among the friends who practice this one-minute samādhi, many have genuinely achieved foreknowledge of the hour and clear right mindfulness at the end)

[Tongren, “fellow practitioners”] is also written as the variant “tongren,” meaning people who work together or share the same calling. [Those who have borne true witness] those who have been truly verified: xìn means “truly”; zhēng means “verification, proof.”

If one does not plan far ahead, trouble will soon be near. “Near trouble” means that it arrives before your very eyes in the twinkling of an eye. In this world, only those with merit and virtue, with wisdom, and with a keen sense of life and death will believe my words. But the pull of the people and affairs right in front of you is too strong; it will make you forget them of itself. Therefore you must be keen, must know what is real and what is false, and must not be deceived by vanity and so let slip the one great matter of this life. Often bring to mind that final day: if it were suddenly before your eyes — how dreadful, how dreadful! You would naturally shudder into wakefulness. This is what is called leaping straight out of the fiery pit.

Ha! Who would believe these two words, “fiery pit”? Little do you know that what most delights you now is precisely what will most torment you later — what is that if not a fiery pit? The Buddha said: “The three realms afford no peace; they are like a burning house.” With a single cut you can awaken at once, and the fiery pit becomes a blue lotus. So simple and direct is it
If you can cut once in moments of terror, you will naturally remain composed and unruffled, and wondrous functioning will unfold.
If you can cut once in moments of anger, you will not be overstimulated, with blood rushing to your head.
If you can cut once in moments of sickness and pain, your fever will abate and you will recover all the sooner.
If you can cut once in moments of sorrow, you will be able to restrain your grief in due measure, and your mind will not be worn away.
If you can cut once at any and every moment, you will naturally attain the joy of light tranquillity and, seeing your true nature, become a Buddha.
Look — what is this? (You may investigate it in ordinary times. But at the very moment of the “slap,” when not a single thought arises, to investigate would itself become delusion.)
Its face — without existence; true emptiness is not empty.
Its dignity — supreme. Above in heaven and below on earth, I alone am the honored one.
Its true reality — not nonexistent; wondrous existence is not existence.
Its form — measureless and boundless, pervading the whole dharma realm.
Its essence — empty, pure, and quiescent, free from birth and death.
Its wonder — everyone has it. Everything is already complete; there is neither ordinary nor holy.
Its function — all-powerful. All things are established through it.
Its standing — the master of all things, and therefore the mother of all Buddhas.
Its nature — defiled, yet ultimately undefiled.
Its distance — for one who sees, it is right before the eyes; for one who does not, it is a thousand mountains and ten thousand rivers away.
